questionText: 8 points on circle. Line segments joining any two?
hints: This is a counting problem. Every line segment joins a pair of points, so you are counting pairs. Be careful not to count the same pair twice.
Start with one point. How many other points can it join to? Then think about whether joining one point to another is the same segment going the other way.
A similar example: with 5 points on a circle, each point joins to 4 others. 5 × 4 = 20, but every segment got counted twice, once from each end. 20 ÷ 2 = 10 line segments.

stepByStep.text: Each of the 8 points can be joined to the 7 other points.
This counts every segment twice, once from each end. So halve it.
You can check by adding the new segments point by point.
There are 28 line segments.

misconceptions.A: This is 8 × 2. Each point joins to 7 others, not 2. Count the pairs of points.
misconceptions.B: 7 is how many segments start from just one point. Count the segments from all the points.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 pairs of points, so there are 28 segments.
misconceptions.D: Check your counting of pairs. Each of the 8 points joins to 7 others, and then you halve because each segment is counted twice.

questionText: A,B,C,D play chess. Each plays 2 games with every other. Total games?
hints: This is a counting problem about pairs. First find how many different pairs of players there are, then think about how many games each pair plays.
List the pairs of players. The first player can pair with three others. Keep going, without repeating any pair.
A similar example: 3 friends each play 2 games with every other friend. The pairs are first and second, first and third, second and third. That is 3 pairs. 3 × 2 = 6 games.

stepByStep.text: Use the players' names to list the pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD. That is 6 pairs.
Each pair plays 2 games.
The total is 12 games.

misconceptions.A: This is 4 players × 2 games. But games are played by pairs, so count the pairs of players first.
misconceptions.B: Check your list of pairs. There are 6 different pairs, and each pair plays 2 games.
misconceptions.C: This is 4 × 4. A player does not play against themselves, and each pair is counted once. Find the 6 pairs first.
misconceptions.D: Yes! There are 6 pairs of players and each pair plays 2 games, so 6 × 2 = 12.

questionText: Points on circle, max 15 line segments. How many points?
hints: This is a counting problem turned around. You know the number of line segments and need the number of points. Remember that each segment joins one pair of points.
Try a small number of points and count the segments. With 3 points you get 3 segments. See how the count grows each time you add one more point.

A similar example: how many points give 10 segments? 2 points give 1 segment. A third point adds 2 more, making 3. A fourth point adds 3 more, and a fifth adds 4 more. 3 + 3 + 4 = 10, so 5 points give 10 segments.

stepByStep.text: Each new point joins to all the points already there. Build up the count one point at a time.
2 points give 1 segment. 3 points give 1 + 2 = 3 segments. 4 points give 3 + 3 = 6 segments.
5 points give 6 + 4 = 10 segments. One more point adds 5 more.
Check another way: 6 points, each joined to 5 others, with each segment counted twice.
So there are 6 points.

misconceptions.A: 4 points give only 6 segments. Keep adding points until you reach 15.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 6 points give 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 segments.
misconceptions.C: 5 points give 10 segments, which is not enough. One more point adds 5 more segments.
misconceptions.D: 7 points give 21 segments, which is more than 15. Try one point fewer.

questionText: Using digits 4,7,6,9 each only once, how many 4-digit odd numbers?
hints: This is a counting problem about arranging digits. An odd number must end in an odd digit, so start by thinking about the last place.
Which of the digits 4, 7, 6 and 9 are odd? Those are the only digits allowed in the ones place. Choose that place first, then fill the other places.

A similar example: using 2, 3 and 8 once each, how many 3-digit even numbers are there? The last digit must be 2 or 8, so 2 choices. The other two digits can go in 2 × 1 = 2 orders. 2 × 2 = 4 even numbers.

stepByStep.text: An odd number ends in an odd digit. Here the odd digits are 7 and 9, so there are 2 choices for the ones place.
The 3 digits left over fill the other three places. They can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.
Multiply the choices together.
There are 12 odd numbers.

misconceptions.A: This would need 3 odd digits to choose from for the last place. Only 7 and 9 are odd, so there are 2 choices.
misconceptions.B: 6 is the count for just one ending digit. The number can end in 7 or in 9, so double it.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 2 choices for the last digit and 6 ways to arrange the rest gives 2 × 6 = 12.
misconceptions.D: Check each place in turn. The last place has 2 choices, then the other places have 3, 2 and 1 choices.

questionText: 15 people meeting, each shakes hands once. Total handshakes?
hints: This is a counting problem about pairs. Each handshake is between two people, so count the pairs. Make sure each handshake is counted only once.
Think about one person first. How many other people do they shake hands with? Then remember that one handshake is shared by two people.
A similar example: 6 people each shake hands once with everyone else. Each person shakes 5 hands. 6 × 5 = 30, but each handshake was counted twice. 30 ÷ 2 = 15 handshakes.

stepByStep.text: Each of the 15 people shakes hands with the 14 others.
Each handshake has been counted twice, once for each person. So halve it.
There are 105 handshakes.

misconceptions.A: Check your multiplication. 15 × 14 = 210, and half of that is the number of handshakes.
misconceptions.B: This is the count for 16 people. Each of the 15 people shakes hands with 14 others, so work out 15 × 14 ÷ 2.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 15 × 14 ÷ 2 = 105 handshakes.
misconceptions.D: Check your sum. Each of the 15 people shakes 14 hands, and every handshake is counted twice, so find 15 × 14 ÷ 2.

questionText: Using digits 1,5,3,7 each once, how many numbers >5000?
hints: This is a counting problem about arranging digits. A 4-digit number is bigger than 5000 only if its first digit is big enough. Start with the thousands place.
Which of the digits 1, 5, 3 and 7 can go in the thousands place so the number is more than 5000? Choose that digit first, then arrange the rest.

A similar example: using 2, 4 and 9 once each, how many 3-digit numbers are bigger than 400? The first digit must be 4 or 9, so 2 choices. The other two digits can go in 2 × 1 = 2 orders. 2 × 2 = 4 numbers.

stepByStep.text: To be more than 5000, the thousands digit must be 5 or 7. That is 2 choices.
The 3 digits left can fill the other places in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.
Multiply the choices.
There are 12 numbers greater than 5000.

misconceptions.A: 24 is how many 4-digit numbers you can make altogether. Only those starting with 5 or 7 are more than 5000.
misconceptions.B: Check each place in turn. The first place has 2 choices, then the other places have 3, 2 and 1 choices.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 2 choices for the first digit and 6 ways to arrange the rest gives 12.
misconceptions.D: This would mean 3 digits can go first. A number starting with 1 or 3 is less than 5000, so only 5 and 7 can go first.

questionText: Using 7,6,9,4 each once, how many 4-digit odd numbers?
hints: This is a counting problem about arranging digits. An odd number must end in an odd digit, so start by thinking about the last place.
Which of the digits 4, 7, 6 and 9 are odd? Those are the only digits allowed in the ones place. Choose that place first, then fill the other places.

A similar example: using 2, 3 and 8 once each, how many 3-digit even numbers are there? The last digit must be 2 or 8, so 2 choices. The other two digits can go in 2 × 1 = 2 orders. 2 × 2 = 4 even numbers.

stepByStep.text: An odd number ends in an odd digit. Here the odd digits are 7 and 9, so there are 2 choices for the ones place.
The 3 digits left over fill the other three places. They can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.
Multiply the choices together.
There are 12 odd numbers.

misconceptions.A: This would need 3 odd digits to choose from for the last place. Only 7 and 9 are odd, so there are 2 choices.
misconceptions.B: 6 is the count for just one ending digit. The number can end in 7 or in 9, so double it.
misconceptions.C: 24 is how many 4-digit numbers there are altogether. Only the ones ending in 7 or 9 are odd, which is half of them.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 2 choices for the last digit and 6 ways to arrange the rest gives 2 × 6 = 12.

questionText: How many whole numbers are there from 15 to 42, counting both 15 and 42?
hints: When you count from one number up to another and both ends are included, think about whether subtracting alone counts every number.
Find 42 − 15 first. Then ask yourself whether the starting number 15 has been counted yet.
A similar problem: from 6 to 10 the numbers are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. Subtracting gives 10 − 6 = 4, and adding 1 for the starting number gives 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Subtract the smaller number from the larger one.
This counts the jumps. Add 1 so that the starting number 15 is counted too.
There are 28 whole numbers from 15 to 42.

misconceptions.A: This is 42 − 15, which counts the jumps between the numbers. Add 1 more so that 15 itself is counted.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 42 − 15 = 27, and one more for the starting number gives 28.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 after subtracting. Only one extra is needed, for the starting number.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out both 15 and 42. The question asks you to count both of them.

questionText: Meera stands in a queue at the school canteen. She is 7th from the front and 5th from the back. How many children are in the queue?
hints: A position from the front and a position from the back both count the same child. Think about what happens if you simply add them.
There are 6 children in front of Meera. Work out how many are behind her, then count Meera once.
A similar problem: Raju is 3rd from the front and 4th from the back. In front of him are 2 children, behind him are 3, and Raju makes 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 children.

stepByStep.text: Count the children in front of Meera and behind her.
Add them, and add Meera herself once.
There are 11 children in the queue.

misconceptions.A: This is 7 + 5, which counts Meera twice. Take 1 away so she is counted only once.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to 7 + 5. Meera has already been counted twice, so 1 must be taken away instead.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 6 in front, 4 behind, and Meera herself make 11.
misconceptions.D: This counts the 6 in front and the 4 behind but leaves out Meera. Remember to count her once.

questionText: A straight fence is 40 metres long. A post stands every 5 metres, with a post at each end. How many posts are there?
hints: Posts stand at the ends of the gaps. In a straight line with a post at both ends, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
First find how many 5-metre gaps fit into 40 metres.
A similar problem: a 12-metre fence with a post every 4 metres has 12 ÷ 4 = 3 gaps. The posts stand at 0, 4, 8 and 12 metres, so there are 4 posts.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of gaps between posts.
A straight line of gaps has one more post than gaps.
There are 9 posts.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 8 gaps need 9 posts, because there is a post at both ends.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of gaps, 40 ÷ 5. The post at the very start still needs to be counted.
misconceptions.C: This takes 1 away from the 8 gaps. With a post at each end, there is one more post than gaps.
misconceptions.D: This adds 2 to the number of gaps. Only one extra post is needed.

questionText: How many 2-digit numbers end in the digit 5?
hints: Think about which digits are allowed in the tens place of a 2-digit number.
Start listing them: 15, 25, 35, and keep going until the last 2-digit number that ends in 5.
A similar problem: the 2-digit numbers smaller than 60 that end in 2 are 12, 22, 32, 42 and 52. The tens digit runs from 1 to 5, so there are 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The ones digit is fixed as 5. The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9.
There are 9 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 itself (or 05) as well. The number 5 has only one digit, so it is not a 2-digit number.
misconceptions.B: This looks like the ending digit, not the count. Try listing the numbers: 15, 25, 35 and so on.
misconceptions.C: One number has been missed. Check that 55 and 95 are both in your list.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! The tens digit can be any of 1 to 9, so there are 9 numbers.

questionText: Riya has 3 different tops and 2 different skirts. An outfit is one top worn with one skirt. How many different outfits can she make?
hints: Every top can be paired with every skirt. Think about how many pairs each top makes.
Take the first top. How many outfits can it make with the 2 skirts? Then do the same for the other tops.
A similar problem: with 4 caps and 2 scarves, each cap can go with 2 scarves, so there are 4 × 2 = 8 pairs.

stepByStep.text: Each top can be worn with either of the 2 skirts, so each top gives 2 outfits.
There are 3 tops.
Riya can make 6 different outfits.

misconceptions.A: This adds 3 + 2. Each top goes with every skirt, so the numbers are multiplied.
misconceptions.B: Great job! Each of the 3 tops makes 2 outfits, so 3 × 2 = 6.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 3. There are only 2 skirts for each top, so it is 3 × 2.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the tops. Each top makes 2 different outfits, one for each skirt.

questionText: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 30?
hints: Even and odd numbers take turns as you count. Think about what share of the numbers are even.
The even numbers start 2, 4, 6. Find the last even number in the range and see which place it holds in the list.
A similar problem: from 1 to 10 the even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Every second number is even, so there are 10 ÷ 2 = 5 of them.

stepByStep.text: From 1 to 30, every second number is even: 2, 4, 6, and so on up to 30.
Half of the 30 numbers are even.
There are 15 even numbers from 1 to 30.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Every second number is even, and 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
misconceptions.B: This leaves out one even number. Check that 30 itself is counted, because 30 is even.
misconceptions.C: This counts one too many. Zero is not in the range 1 to 30, so the list starts at 2.
misconceptions.D: This is how many numbers there are altogether. Only every second one is even.

questionText: A carpenter cuts a long wooden plank into 6 pieces. He cuts one piece at a time. How many cuts does he make?
hints: Think about what one cut does to the number of pieces.
Before any cut there is 1 piece. After the first cut there are 2 pieces. Keep going until there are 6.
A similar problem: to cut a ribbon into 3 pieces, the first cut makes 2 pieces and the second cut makes 3 pieces. So 2 cuts are needed.

stepByStep.text: The plank starts as 1 piece. Every cut adds 1 more piece.
To reach 6 pieces, 5 more pieces are needed.
The carpenter makes 5 cuts.

misconceptions.A: This matches the number of pieces. The plank is already 1 piece before any cut, so one cut fewer is needed.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to the number of pieces. Cuts are one fewer than pieces, not one more.
misconceptions.C: You got it! Each cut adds one piece, so 5 cuts turn 1 piece into 6.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the pieces. Try it with a paper strip: each cut makes just one extra piece.

questionText: How many different 2-digit numbers can you make using only the digits 3 and 8? A digit may be used twice in a number.
hints: Think about the choices for the tens place and the choices for the ones place.
Write the numbers that start with 3 first. Then write the ones that start with 8.
A similar problem: with the digits 1, 2 and 5 and repeats allowed, there are 3 choices for the tens place and 3 for the ones place, so 3 × 3 = 9 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit can be 3 or 8, and the ones digit can be 3 or 8.
That gives 2 choices for each place.
The numbers are 33, 38, 83 and 88, so 4 numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This counts only 38 and 83. A digit may be used twice, so 33 and 88 count too.
misconceptions.B: One number has been missed. Check your list for 33, 38, 83 and 88.
misconceptions.C: This is more than can be made. With 2 choices for each of the 2 places there are 2 × 2 numbers.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 33, 38, 83 and 88 make 4 numbers.

questionText: The pages of a small story book are numbered from 1 to 25. How many digits are printed in all to number the pages?
hints: Some page numbers have one digit and some have two. Count the two groups separately.
Pages 1 to 9 use one digit each. Work out how many pages are left from 10 to 25.
A similar problem: for pages 1 to 12, pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Pages 10, 11 and 12 are 3 pages using 2 digits each, which is 6 digits. In all, 9 + 6 = 15 digits.

stepByStep.text: Pages 1 to 9 have one digit each.
Pages 10 to 25 are 16 pages with two digits each.
Add the two groups.
In all, 41 digits are printed.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 9 digits for pages 1 to 9 and 32 digits for pages 10 to 25 make 41.
misconceptions.B: This gives two digits to every page. Pages 1 to 9 have only one digit each.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of pages, not the number of digits. Pages from 10 onwards use two digits each.
misconceptions.D: This is 9 + 25. Count only the pages from 10 to 25 as two-digit pages: there are 16 of them, and each uses 2 digits.

questionText: How many 2-digit numbers have digits that add up to 7?
hints: Work in an organised way: choose the tens digit first, and the ones digit is then decided.
Start with tens digit 1. The ones digit must be 6, giving 16. Now try tens digit 2, and carry on.
A similar problem: 2-digit numbers with digits adding to 4 are 13, 22, 31 and 40. The tens digit runs from 1 to 4, so there are 4 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7. It cannot be 0.
For each tens digit there is exactly one ones digit that makes the total 7.
The numbers are 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70.
There are 7 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been left out. Remember 70, because 7 + 0 = 7.
misconceptions.B: This also counts 07. That is just 7, which has only one digit.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70 are the 7 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the count. Each tens digit from 1 to 7 gives just one number.

questionText: Kiran writes all the numbers from 1 to 40 in her notebook. How many times does she write the digit 3?
hints: A digit can appear in the ones place or in the tens place. Count each place separately.
First list the numbers that have 3 in the ones place: 3, 13, and so on. Then look at the numbers that have 3 in the tens place.

A similar problem: from 1 to 30, the digit 2 is in the ones place in 2, 12 and 22, which is 3 times. It is in the tens place in 20 to 29, which is 10 times. In all it is written 13 times, and 22 is counted twice because it has two 2s.

stepByStep.text: In the ones place, 3 appears in 3, 13, 23 and 33.
In the tens place, 3 appears in 30, 31, 32, and so on up to 39.
Add the two counts. The number 33 has two 3s, so it is rightly counted in both.
She writes the digit 3 a total of 14 times.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the ones place. The numbers 30 to 39 each have a 3 in the tens place too.
misconceptions.B: This counts 33 only once. It has two 3s, and the question asks how many times the digit is written.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the tens place. The numbers 3, 13, 23 and 33 also have a 3 in the ones place.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 4 times in the ones place and 10 times in the tens place make 14.

questionText: 30 children stand in a line for the morning assembly. Arjun is 12th from the front. What is his position from the back?
hints: Find how many children stand behind him. His place from the back is one more than that.
Arjun is 12th from the front, so take 12 away from 30 to find how many children are behind him.
A similar problem: in a line of 10 children, Sita is 4th from the front. Behind her are 10 − 4 = 6 children, so she is 7th from the back.

stepByStep.text: Find how many children are behind Arjun.
Counting from the back, those 18 children come first and Arjun is next.
Arjun is 19th from the back.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of children behind Arjun. He comes just after them, so his position is one more.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 18 children are behind him, so Arjun is 19th from the back.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 to the 18 children behind him. Only Arjun himself needs to be added, which is 1.
misconceptions.D: This adds 30 and 12. A position in the line cannot be bigger than the number of children.

questionText: A square garden has sides of 12 metres. Posts are fixed all around its edge, one at every corner and one every 3 metres along each side. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go all the way around and come back to the start. In a closed loop, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
Find the distance all the way around the garden first. Then see how many 3-metre gaps fit into it.
A similar problem: a square of side 6 metres with a post every 2 metres has a distance around of 24 metres. That is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 gaps, and going around a loop needs exactly 12 posts.

stepByStep.text: Find the distance around the garden.
Find the number of 3-metre gaps.
Around a closed loop the last gap ends at the first post, so the number of posts equals the number of gaps.
16 posts are needed.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 posts on each of the 4 sides. Each corner post then gets counted twice, once for each side it joins.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to the 16 gaps, as for a straight fence. Around a loop the last post is the first post again.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! 48 metres around gives 16 gaps, and a loop needs 16 posts.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the 3 posts in the middle of each side. The 4 corner posts must be added.

questionText: Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row for a photo. In how many different orders can they stand?
hints: Think place by place: who can stand first, then who can stand next, then who is left.
Suppose Anu stands first. Write the orders the other two can stand in. Then let Binu stand first, and then Charu.
A similar problem: two friends, Raj and Sam, can stand as Raj then Sam, or Sam then Raj. There are 2 choices for the first place and 1 for the second, so 2 × 1 = 2 orders.

stepByStep.text: Any of the 3 children can stand first.
Once the first is chosen, 2 children are left for the second place, and then 1 for the last place.
Multiply the choices.
They can stand in 6 different orders.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 × 3. After one child takes the first place, only 2 are left for the next place.
misconceptions.B: This counts only who stands first. For each first child, the other two can stand in 2 ways.
misconceptions.C: Some orders have been missed. List them by first child: each child can be first in 2 orders.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 3 choices, then 2, then 1 give 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders.

questionText: A window has 4 small square panes, arranged as 2 rows of 2. Counting squares of every size, how many squares can you see in the window?
hints: Squares can be of different sizes. Count the small ones, then look for bigger squares made by joining small ones.
Count the small panes first. Then ask whether all four panes together make a square.
A similar problem: a single square pane has just 1 square. A row of 2 panes has 2 small squares and no bigger square, because the two together make a long rectangle. So it has 2 squares.

stepByStep.text: There are 4 small square panes.
The whole window, made of all 4 panes, is 1 big square.
Add them.
There are 5 squares in the window.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 4 small squares and 1 big square make 5.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the small panes. The whole window is a square too.
misconceptions.C: This counts one square too many. Two panes side by side make a rectangle, not a square.
misconceptions.D: This counts the pairs of panes as squares. Two panes joined together are longer than they are tall, so they are rectangles.

questionText: 16 players enter a knockout badminton tournament. In every match the loser goes out and the winner plays on. How many matches are played to find the champion?
hints: Each match sends exactly one player out. Think about how many players must go out before one champion is left.
Count round by round: 16 players play 8 matches in the first round, leaving 8 players. Carry on until one player is left.
A similar problem: with 4 players, the first round has 2 matches and the final is 1 match. That is 2 + 1 = 3 matches, and 3 players have gone out.

stepByStep.text: Count the matches in each round.
Another way to see it: each match sends one player out, and 15 players must go out to leave 1 champion.
15 matches are played.

misconceptions.A: This is only the first round. The 8 winners must keep playing until one champion is left.
misconceptions.B: This matches the number of players. The champion never loses, so there is one match fewer.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 matches, one for each player who goes out.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of rounds. Each round has several matches, so add up the matches in all the rounds.

questionText: How many 2-digit numbers are multiples of 7?
hints: Find the smallest and the largest 2-digit multiples, then count how many multiples lie from one to the other.
The first multiple of 7 with two digits is 14, which is 7 × 2. Find the largest multiple of 7 that is below 100.
A similar problem: the 2-digit multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60 and 80. They are 20 × 1 up to 20 × 4, so there are 4 of them.

stepByStep.text: The smallest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 14.
The largest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 98.
Count the multipliers from 2 to 14.
There are 13 two-digit multiples of 7.

misconceptions.A: This counts all multiples of 7 up to 98, including 7 itself. The number 7 has only one digit.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The multiples run from 7 × 2 to 7 × 14, which is 13 numbers.
misconceptions.C: This takes away one too many. From 7 × 2 to 7 × 14 there are 14 − 2 + 1 multipliers.
misconceptions.D: This counts too many. 7 × 15 = 105 has three digits, and 7 × 1 = 7 has one digit.

questionText: Sunita walks up from the 1st floor to the 4th floor and climbs 48 steps. Every floor has the same number of steps. How many steps would she climb from the 1st floor to the 7th floor?
hints: Going from one floor to another, count the flights of stairs climbed, not the floor numbers.
From the 1st floor to the 4th floor Sunita climbs 3 flights of stairs. Use this to find the steps in one flight.
A similar problem: going from the 1st floor to the 3rd floor is 2 flights. If that is 20 steps, each flight has 10 steps. From the 1st floor to the 5th floor is 4 flights, which is 40 steps.

stepByStep.text: From the 1st to the 4th floor there are 3 flights of stairs.
Find the steps in one flight.
From the 1st to the 7th floor there are 6 flights.
She would climb 96 steps.

misconceptions.A: This divides 48 by 4 and multiplies by 7. Starting on the 1st floor, reaching the 4th floor takes only 3 flights.
misconceptions.B: This uses 16 steps per flight, which is right, but counts 7 flights. From the 1st floor to the 7th there are 6 flights.
misconceptions.C: This uses 6 flights, which is right, but divides 48 by 4. The 48 steps are shared among 3 flights.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Each flight has 16 steps, and 6 flights make 96 steps.

questionText: An ice-cream shop has 4 flavours: mango, chocolate, vanilla and strawberry. Rohan picks 2 different flavours for his cup. How many different pairs of flavours can he choose?
hints: A pair is the same whichever flavour is named first. List the pairs in an organised way so that none is repeated.
Start with mango and pair it with each of the other three. Then move to chocolate, pairing it only with flavours not used with it before.
A similar problem: from 3 fruits, apple, banana and cherry, the pairs are apple-banana, apple-cherry and banana-cherry. That is 2 + 1 = 3 pairs.

stepByStep.text: Mango can pair with chocolate, vanilla or strawberry: 3 pairs.
Chocolate can pair with vanilla or strawberry: 2 new pairs. Vanilla can pair with strawberry: 1 new pair.
Add the pairs.
Rohan can choose 6 different pairs.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 pairs.
misconceptions.B: This is 4 × 3, which counts mango with chocolate and chocolate with mango as two pairs. In a cup they are the same pair, so halve it.
misconceptions.C: This is 4 × 2. Try listing the pairs: mango goes with 3 others, chocolate with 2 new ones, vanilla with 1 new one.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of flavours. Each pair uses two flavours, so list the pairs to count them.

questionText: Using each of the digits 2, 0 and 5 exactly once, how many 3-digit numbers can be made?
hints: Look carefully at the hundreds place. One of these digits cannot go there.
A 3-digit number cannot begin with 0. So the hundreds digit is 2 or 5. List the numbers that begin with 2 first.
A similar problem: with the digits 0 and 7 used once each, 07 is just 7, so the only 2-digit number is 70. That is 1 number, not 2.

stepByStep.text: The hundreds digit can be 2 or 5, but not 0.
Starting with 2: 205 and 250. Starting with 5: 502 and 520.
Count them.
4 three-digit numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 × 2 × 1, which also counts 025 and 052. Those begin with 0, so they are really 2-digit numbers.
misconceptions.B: One number has been missed. For each of the two possible hundreds digits there are 2 numbers.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 205, 250, 502 and 520 are the 4 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This counts the choices for the hundreds place only. Each choice gives 2 different numbers.

questionText: A big triangle has two straight lines drawn from its top corner down to its base. These lines split it into 3 small triangles side by side. Counting triangles of every size, how many triangles are there in the figure?
hints: Count the small triangles first, then triangles made by joining neighbouring small ones.
There are 3 small triangles. Next, count the triangles made of 2 small triangles that are next to each other.
A similar problem: one line from the top corner to the base splits a triangle into 2 small triangles. Together with the big one, that makes 2 + 1 = 3 triangles.

stepByStep.text: There are 3 small triangles.
Two neighbouring small triangles together make a bigger triangle. This can be done in 2 ways: left with middle, and middle with right.
All three together make the 1 big triangle.
Add them all.
There are 6 triangles in the figure.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the small triangles. Neighbouring ones join to make bigger triangles too.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 3 small, 2 made of two parts, and 1 big one make 6.
misconceptions.C: One triangle has been missed. Check the two-part triangles: left with middle, and middle with right.
misconceptions.D: This counts the small triangles and the big one. Two neighbouring small triangles also make a triangle.

questionText: In a ticket queue at the railway station, Ravi is 8th from the front and Sana is 15th from the front. How many people stand between them?
hints: The people between them hold the positions after Ravi and before Sana. Neither Ravi nor Sana is counted.
List the positions between them, starting 9th, 10th, and stopping just before the 15th.
A similar problem: between the 3rd and the 6th person stand the 4th and the 5th. Subtracting gives 6 − 3 = 3, and taking 1 away gives 2 people.

stepByStep.text: The people between them are at positions 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
A quick way: subtract the positions and take away 1.
6 people stand between them.

misconceptions.A: This is 15 − 8, which counts Sana as well. Take 1 away so that only the people in between are counted.
misconceptions.B: This adds the two positions. To find who is between them, look at the positions from 9th to 14th.
misconceptions.C: This counts both Ravi and Sana along with the people between them. Count only positions 9 to 14.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Positions 9 to 14 hold 6 people.

questionText: How many numbers from 100 to 200, counting both 100 and 200, end in the digit 0?
hints: Numbers ending in 0 come once in every ten numbers. Be careful with both ends of the range.
List them: 100, 110, 120, and keep going. Check whether 200 belongs in your list.
A similar problem: from 10 to 50, the numbers ending in 0 are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. There are 4 jumps of ten, and 4 + 1 = 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: From 100 to 200 there are 10 jumps of ten, and one more for the starting number.
There are 11 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Ten jumps of ten from 100 to 200 give 11 numbers.
misconceptions.B: This counts the jumps of ten. Both 100 and 200 are in the range, so there is one more number than jumps.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out both 100 and 200. The question says to count both.
misconceptions.D: This counts too many. Only one number in every ten ends in 0.

questionText: The pages of a book are numbered starting from 1. In all, 129 digits were printed for the page numbers. How many pages does the book have?
hints: Work backwards. Take away the digits used by the one-digit pages, then see how many two-digit pages the remaining digits can number.
Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Subtract these from 129 to find the digits left for pages with two digits.
A similar problem: a booklet uses 29 digits. Pages 1 to 9 use 9, leaving 20 digits. That numbers 20 ÷ 2 = 10 two-digit pages, so the booklet has 9 + 10 = 19 pages.

stepByStep.text: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Find the digits left.
Each page from 10 onwards uses 2 digits.
Add the one-digit pages and the two-digit pages.
The book has 69 pages.

misconceptions.A: This halves 129 as if every page used two digits. Pages 1 to 9 use only one digit each.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 9 one-digit pages and 60 two-digit pages make 69 pages.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of two-digit pages only. The 9 one-digit pages must be added.
misconceptions.D: This adds 10 one-digit pages. The one-digit pages are 1 to 9, which is 9 pages.

questionText: How many 2-digit numbers have a tens digit that is bigger than the ones digit? For example, 72 is such a number but 27 is not.
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the tens digit and count the ones digits that are smaller than it. Look for a pattern.
With tens digit 1, the only smaller ones digit is 0, giving 10. With tens digit 2, the ones digit can be 0 or 1. Carry on up to tens digit 9.
A similar problem: among numbers from 10 to 39, tens digit 1 gives 1 number (10), tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers (20, 21) and tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers (30, 31, 32). That is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Tens digit 1 gives 1 number (10). Tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers (20, 21). Tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers, and so on.
Tens digit 9 gives 9 numbers (90 to 98).
Add the counts.
There are 45 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the numbers with ones digit 0, such as 10, 20 and 30. Zero is smaller than every tens digit.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 + 2 + 3 up to 10. The largest tens digit is 9, so the adding stops at 9.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 9 = 45.
misconceptions.D: This only removes the 9 numbers with equal digits, like 11 and 22. Numbers such as 27, where the tens digit is smaller, must also be left out.

questionText: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 4?
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the hundreds digit, then count the ways the other two digits can make up the rest.
Start with hundreds digit 1. The other two digits must add up to 3. List these numbers, then move on to hundreds digit 2.
A similar problem: 3-digit numbers with digits adding to 2 are 101, 110 and 200. Hundreds digit 1 gives 2 numbers and hundreds digit 2 gives 1 number, so there are 3.

stepByStep.text: Hundreds digit 1: the other digits add to 3, giving 103, 112, 121 and 130. That is 4 numbers.
Hundreds digit 2: 202, 211 and 220. That is 3 numbers.
Hundreds digit 3: 301 and 310. Hundreds digit 4: 400. That is 2 numbers and 1 number.
Add the counts.
There are 10 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been missed. Check for 400, where the digits are 4, 0 and 0.
misconceptions.B: This also counts numbers like 013 and 004 that begin with 0. Those are not 3-digit numbers.
misconceptions.C: This only arranges the digits 1, 0 and 3. Other sets of digits also add up to 4, such as 1, 1, 2 and 2, 2, 0.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 numbers.

questionText: A square board is divided into 9 small squares, in 3 rows of 3. Counting squares of every size, how many squares are there on the board?
hints: Squares come in different sizes. Count each size separately: the smallest, the middle size, and the largest.
There are 9 small squares. Now count the squares that are 2 small squares wide and 2 tall. One sits in each corner of the board.
A similar problem: a board with 2 rows of 2 has 4 small squares and 1 big square, so 4 + 1 = 5 squares.

stepByStep.text: There are 9 small squares.
Squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall: one fits in each corner of the board, so there are 4.
The whole board is 1 large square.
Add all the sizes.
There are 14 squares on the board.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 9 small, 4 middle-sized and 1 large make 14.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the small squares. Bigger squares are made by joining small ones.
misconceptions.C: This counts the small squares and the whole board. There are also 4 squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the whole board, which is the largest square of all.

questionText: Four small squares are joined in a single row to make a long strip. Counting rectangles of every size, with the small squares counted too, how many rectangles are there in the strip?
hints: A rectangle in the strip is made of 1, 2, 3 or 4 neighbouring squares. Count each length separately.
There are 4 rectangles made of 1 square. Next, count the rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: first with second, second with third, and so on.
A similar problem: a strip of 3 squares has 3 rectangles of one square, 2 of two squares and 1 of three squares. That is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 rectangles.

stepByStep.text: Rectangles made of 1 square: 4.
Rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: 3. Made of 3 neighbouring squares: 2.
The whole strip of 4 squares: 1.
Add them.
There are 10 rectangles in the strip.

misconceptions.A: This counts the single squares and the pairs. Rectangles made of 3 squares and the whole strip count too.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 rectangles.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the small squares. Neighbouring squares join to make longer rectangles.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the whole strip, which is the longest rectangle.

questionText: At a birthday party, every child gave one card to every other child. In all, 30 cards were given. How many children were at the party?
hints: Each child gives a card to everyone except themselves. So the total is the number of children times one less than that number.
Try a small party: with 3 children, each gives 2 cards. Work out the total for 4 children, then 5, and keep going until you reach 30.
A similar problem: if 12 cards were given, try 4 children. Each gives 3 cards, and 4 × 3 = 12. So there were 4 children.

stepByStep.text: If there are some children, each one gives a card to all the others, which is one fewer than the number of children.
Look for two numbers next to each other that multiply to 30.
So 6 children each gave 5 cards.
There were 6 children at the party.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of cards each child gave. The number of children is one more than that.
misconceptions.B: This halves 30, as for handshakes. A card goes one way only, so every card is counted just once.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 6 children giving 5 cards each makes 30 cards.
misconceptions.D: With 10 children, each would give 9 cards, making 90 cards. Look for two neighbouring numbers that multiply to 30.

questionText: Using the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3, with no digit repeated in a number, how many 3-digit even numbers can be made?
hints: Two places need care: the ones place must make the number even, and the hundreds place cannot be 0. Split into cases by the last digit.
An even number here ends in 0 or 2. First count the numbers that end in 0. The other two places are filled from 1, 2 and 3.
A similar problem: 2-digit even numbers from the digits 0, 3 and 4 with no repeats. Ending in 0: 30 and 40. Ending in 4: only 34, because 04 is not a 2-digit number. That is 2 + 1 = 3 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Ending in 0: the hundreds digit has 3 choices (1, 2 or 3) and the tens digit then has 2 choices.
Ending in 2: the hundreds digit can only be 1 or 3, and the tens digit then has 2 choices.
Add the two cases.
10 such numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This allows 0 in the hundreds place for numbers ending in 2, such as 012 and 032. Those are not 3-digit numbers.
misconceptions.B: Some numbers ending in 2 have been missed. They are 102, 132, 302 and 312.
misconceptions.C: This is the count of all 3-digit numbers that can be made. Only those ending in 0 or 2 are even.
misconceptions.D: Great job! 6 numbers end in 0 and 4 end in 2, making 10.

questionText: A temple bell takes 6 seconds to ring 4 times, measured from the first ring to the last ring. The rings are evenly spaced. How many seconds does it take to ring 10 times?
hints: The time is spent in the gaps between the rings, not on the rings themselves. Count the gaps.
Between 4 rings there are 3 gaps. Use this to find how long one gap lasts.
A similar problem: a bell takes 8 seconds to ring 3 times. That is 2 gaps, so each gap is 4 seconds. Ringing 6 times has 5 gaps, which takes 5 × 4 = 20 seconds.

stepByStep.text: 4 rings have 3 gaps between them. Find the length of one gap.
10 rings have 9 gaps between them.
Multiply the gaps by the length of each gap.
It takes 18 seconds to ring 10 times.

misconceptions.A: This divides 6 seconds by 4 rings. The time is taken by the 3 gaps between the rings, so each gap is 2 seconds.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! 9 gaps of 2 seconds each take 18 seconds.
misconceptions.C: This uses 2 seconds per gap, which is right, but counts 10 gaps. Between 10 rings there are only 9 gaps.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the 6 seconds. Count the gaps instead: 4 rings have 3 gaps and 10 rings have 9 gaps.

questionText: Children stand in a row. Tara is 9th from the left and Uma is 6th from the right. They swap places, and now Tara is 15th from the left. How many children are in the row?
hints: After the swap, Tara stands exactly where Uma stood. So you know one spot's position from both ends.
Uma's old spot is 6th from the right. After the swap Tara is in that spot, and it is 15th from the left. Use both positions for this one spot.
A similar problem: a spot is 4th from the left and 3rd from the right. There are 3 children to its left and 2 to its right, so the row has 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 children.

stepByStep.text: After swapping, Tara stands in Uma's old spot. That spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right.
Add the two positions and take away 1, because the spot is counted twice.
There are 20 children in the row.

misconceptions.A: This adds 15 and 6 but counts the child in that spot twice. Take 1 away.
misconceptions.B: This is Tara's new position from the left. There are still 5 more children to her right.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The same spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right, so 15 + 6 − 1 = 20.
misconceptions.D: This adds Tara's old and new positions, 9 and 15. Use the two positions of the same spot instead: 15th from the left and 6th from the right.

questionText: Aman writes all the numbers from 1 to 100. How many times does he write the digit 1?
hints: Count place by place: how often the digit is in the ones place, in the tens place, and in the hundreds place.
In the ones place the digit 1 appears in 1, 11, 21, and so on up to 91. Count these first, then look at the tens place.
A similar problem: from 1 to 50, the digit 4 is in the ones place 5 times (4, 14, 24, 34, 44) and in the tens place 10 times (40 to 49). That makes 15 times.

stepByStep.text: Tens place: 10, 11, 12, and so on up to 19.
Hundreds place: only in 100.
Add them.
Aman writes the digit 1 a total of 21 times.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 10 in the ones place, 10 in the tens place and 1 in the number 100 make 21.
misconceptions.B: This leaves out the 1 in 100. The number 100 is in the list too.
misconceptions.C: This counts 11 only once and leaves out 100. The number 11 has two 1s, and both are written.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the ones place and the 1 in 100. The numbers 10 to 19 each have a 1 in the tens place as well.

questionText: How many numbers from 1 to 60 can be divided exactly by 2 or by 3, or by both?
hints: Some numbers can be divided by both 2 and 3. If you count the two groups and add, those numbers get counted twice.
Count the multiples of 2 up to 60, and the multiples of 3 up to 60. Then find how many numbers are in both lists.
A similar problem: from 1 to 12 there are 6 multiples of 2 and 4 multiples of 3. The numbers 6 and 12 are in both lists. So the count is 6 + 4 − 2 = 8.

stepByStep.text: Count the multiples of 2 and the multiples of 3.
Numbers in both lists are the multiples of 6.
Add the two lists and take away the numbers counted twice.
There are 40 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This adds 30 and 20, which counts the multiples of 6 twice. Take away those 10 numbers.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the multiples of 2. Odd multiples of 3, such as 3, 9 and 15, belong too.
misconceptions.C: This is how many numbers are divisible by both 2 and 3. The question also wants numbers divisible by just one of them.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 30 + 20 − 10 = 40.

questionText: A flag has 3 stripes in a row. Each stripe is painted red, green or blue. Stripes that touch each other must be different colours. How many different flags can be made?
hints: Choose the colours stripe by stripe. Read the rule with care: only stripes that touch must differ.
The first stripe can be any of the 3 colours. The second stripe must differ from the first. Think about how many colours the third stripe can take.
A similar problem: a flag with 2 stripes and 3 colours, where the stripes must differ. The first stripe has 3 choices and the second has 2, so there are 3 × 2 = 6 flags.

stepByStep.text: The first stripe can be any of 3 colours.
The second stripe touches the first, so it has 2 choices.
The third stripe touches only the second, so it also has 2 choices. It may match the first stripe.
Multiply the choices.
12 different flags can be made.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 flags.
misconceptions.B: This makes all three stripes different. The first and third stripes do not touch, so they may be the same colour.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 3 × 3, which lets touching stripes share a colour. The second and third stripes each have only 2 choices.
misconceptions.D: This is 3 × 3. Count the choices for each stripe in turn: 3, then 2, then 2.

questionText: A, B, C and D are playing chess. Each of the 4 players played two games with every other player. How many games of chess were played altogether?
hints: This is from the 2016 IPM exam (Q17).
Think carefully about what the question is asking.
Try working backwards from the options.

stepByStep.text: Correct answer: Option 1 — 12

misconceptions.B: Common incorrect choice
misconceptions.C: Common incorrect choice
misconceptions.D: Common incorrect choice

questionText: There are some points drawn on the circumference of the circle. The teacher draws a maximum of 15 line segments joining any two of the points. How many points were on the circle?
hints: This is from the 2018 IPM exam (Q12).
Break the problem into smaller steps.
Check your answer by substituting back.

stepByStep.text: Correct answer: Option 2 — 6

misconceptions.A: Common incorrect choice
misconceptions.C: Common incorrect choice
misconceptions.D: Common incorrect choice

questionText: Eight points, named A to H, are marked on the circumference of a circle. How many line segments can be drawn by joining any two of these points?
hints: Count in an organised way so that no segment is missed and none is counted twice. Start from one point and move on to the next.
From A you can draw a segment to each of the other 7 points. From B, the segment to A is already drawn, so count only the new ones. Carry on like this.
Similar example: with 5 points A to E, A joins 4 others, B joins 3 new ones, C joins 2 new ones and D joins 1 new one. 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 segments.

stepByStep.text: From A, draw a segment to each of the other 7 points.
From B there are 6 new segments, from C there are 5, and so on down to 1 new segment from G.
Add them all up.
So 28 line segments can be drawn.

misconceptions.B: 8 is the number of points, and also the number of segments joining only neighbours around the circle. Every point can be joined to points further away too.
misconceptions.C: Each point joins 7 others, not 2. Count 7 from A, then 6 new ones from B, and keep going.
misconceptions.D: Close, but a few segments are missing. Add 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 carefully.

questionText: 5 points are marked on a circle. How many chords can be drawn by joining these points?
hints: Each chord connects 2 points. How many ways can you choose 2 points from 5?
Count systematically: Point A connects to B, C, D, E (4 chords). Point B to C, D, E (3 new). Point C to D, E (2 new). Point D to E (1 new).

stepByStep.text: From A: 4 chords. From B: 3 new. From C: 2 new. From D: 1 new.
Total = 10 chords
Formula: ⁵C₂ = 5!/(2!×3!) = 10

misconceptions.A: Missed some pairs
misconceptions.B: 5 would be if you only joined adjacent points
misconceptions.C: 20 = counted each chord twice (A→B and B→A are the same chord)
